name: Axokine
lead: Axokine is a modified recombinant form of human ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) that was developed as an obesity drug by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals. It carries a 15-amino-acid C-terminal truncation and two substitutions, and is reported to be more potent and stable than natural CNTF [7]. It was designed to reduce body weight through a leptin-like mechanism [4]. Its appearance relevance is fat loss: a drug that lowers appetite and body weight would change body shape and facial leanness.

The weight-loss effect was discovered when CNTF given for motor neuron disease caused unexpected weight loss [7]. In phase III obesity trials around 2003, the average effect was small. According to Wikipedia, patients without antibodies lost about 12.5 pounds over a year versus 4.5 pounds on placebo, while nearly 70 percent developed antibodies to the drug after about three months [7]. It was not commercialised [7].

Axokine is not an appearance product, and it was never sold. It sits in the history of fat-loss pharmacology: bodybuilding and diet forums discussed it in 2001-2002 as a leptin-pathway drug in trials [15][16][17], and later reviews list it among the investigational agents of the early 2000s [4][13].

paras: CNTF was first tested in the 1990s as a possible treatment for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; it did not improve muscle control as much as hoped, but participants reported reduced appetite.[10] A 2001 human study of CNTF for motor neuron disease showed unexpected, substantial weight loss, and further work suggested it cut food intake without causing hunger or stress, possibly through a pathway separate from leptin.[10] Regeneron developed Axokine, a CNTF with a 15-amino-acid truncation and two substitutions, reported as three to five times more potent than CNTF and more stable.[10]

Regeneron reported its phase III results on 31 March 2003.[10] Among the minority of participants who did not develop antibodies, average weight loss was 12.5 pounds over a year compared with 4.5 pounds on placebo, at a daily subcutaneous dose given in the trial; nearly 70 percent developed antibodies after about three months.[10] A Xencor patent application published in 2005 raised the concern that such antibodies might interfere with the body's own CNTF and proposed analogues with lower immunogenicity.[10] The drug was never commercialised.[10]

The route from Axokine to appearance runs through body fat. Facial leanness, a defined jawline and body composition all depend partly on how much fat a person carries, so a drug that lowered appetite and weight in trials was of interest to people wanting a leaner look. Regeneron developed it as a treatment for obesity and associated complications such as type 2 diabetes, not as a cosmetic product [11]. Because it was never approved or marketed, it is not part of any current looksmaxxing routine.

CNTF is a survival factor for neurons and acts through gp130/LIFR signalling and the Jak-STAT pathway in cells such as retinal neurons [2][5]. In db/db mice, the modified CNTF (Axokine) was reported to improve diabetic parameters and hepatic steatosis and to increase basal metabolic rate, in contrast with earlier work in which weight loss was mainly attributed to reduced food intake [4]. A separate study found CNTF prevented acute lipid-induced insulin resistance in peripheral tissues [8]. Axokine was listed among investigational anti-obesity agents in a 2004 review [3].

CNTF signals through a receptor complex of the CNTF receptor alpha subunit with gp130 and the LIF receptor. A 2024 paper reported that Axokine's parent molecule can also act through the oncostatin M receptor, and noted that clinical development of Axokine was halted by the emergence of CNTF antibodies [14]. The same paper describes a chimeric cytokine, IC7, built on an interleukin-6 framework with the CNTF-derived LIFR-binding site, which protected mice from obesity and insulin resistance, and engineered successors designed to avoid CNTF itself [14]. Researchers have therefore continued to pursue the pathway with molecules that do not rely on CNTF.

Reviews from the mid-2000s place Axokine within a wave of investigational anti-obesity agents. A 2004 review grouped it with leptin, insulin and central-nervous-system pathway agents alongside leptin analogues, neuropeptide Y antagonists and melanocortin agonists [4]. A 2005 review on paediatric pharmacotherapy named it, with rimonabant, as one of the few new substances at an advanced stage, noting that sibutramine and orlistat were then the main approved options [12]. A 2007 review described the approved drugs as moderately effective, for example sibutramine reducing body weight by roughly 4-5 kg and orlistat by about 3 kg, which motivated the search for new compounds [13].
The original 2003 drug profile described Axokine as a second-generation neurotrophic factor related to CNTF, in development for obesity and type 2 diabetes [11].

Human data in the sources come mainly from Wikipedia's account of the trials: phase III obesity trials run by Regeneron around 2003 showed a modest effect in patients who did not develop antibodies, and antibody formation in a large majority of participants was a major problem [7]. An earlier trial in ALS produced less improvement in muscle control than expected, along with appetite loss [7]. Cosmetic or body-composition outcomes beyond weight have not been reported.

Published reviews from 2003 to 2007 described Axokine as under development for obesity and type 2 diabetes and as one of the leading investigational agents of its time [11][4][12][13]. A forum post from 2001 shows how recruitment to the phase III study reached the public: a user described being offered a place in a late-stage Axokine trial for weight loss [15]. A 2024 review of the pathway states that development stopped because antibodies to CNTF appeared [14].

CNTF and analogues were also studied for retinal degeneration. A 1998 mouse study tested several survival factors on degenerating photoreceptors [1], and repeated injections of a CNTF analogue were reported to give long-term photoreceptor survival in hereditary retinal degeneration in animals [9]. Wikipedia describes an implant, NT-501, secreting CNTF that reduced photoreceptor degradation in retinitis pigmentosa [7].

timeline.event: CNTF tested for ALS; participants report reduced appetite [10].
Unexpected weight loss noticed in a CNTF motor neuron disease study [10]; forum users begin discussing Axokine [17].
Regeneron reports phase III results: modest weight loss in antibody-negative patients, antibodies in about 70 percent [10].
Xencor patent application raises concern about antibodies cross-reacting with natural CNTF [10].
Engineered IL-6-based cytokines developed to reach the CNTF pathway without CNTF [14].

lore.intro: Axokine appeared on bodybuilding forums in 2001-2002 as a drug that acts on the leptin pathway [16][17].

claims.claim: Axokine works through the same pathway as leptin and causes profound weight loss in humans
claims.believers: A 2002 T Nation poster pointed readers to Regeneron's work, saying the drug works through the same biochemical pathway as leptin and bypasses leptin resistance [16][17].
claims.experts: Regeneron's phase III trials showed an average of 12.5 lb lost over a year in antibody-negative patients versus 4.5 lb on placebo, and antibodies developed in about 70 percent of patients [10]. A 2024 paper reports that antibodies halted development [14].

card.summary: A discontinued CNTF-based injectable for obesity that produced small weight loss in trials and triggered antibodies in most users.
card.note: Never commercialised; antibodies in about 70 percent of trial participants.

quick.overview:
Axokine is a modified version of CNTF, a nerve survival protein, that Regeneron developed for obesity after weight loss was noticed in an earlier trial.

In phase III trials the effect was modest, and most participants developed antibodies. It was not commercialised.
quick.mechanism: It was designed to lower body weight through a leptin-like mechanism, and in diabetic mice it was reported to raise metabolic rate beyond its effect on food intake.
quick.risks: Antibody formation against the drug was the major issue reported in trials. It is not an approved or marketed drug.
